en: End of 2023. In her scenario, your job is to train a 405-billion-parameter model in four months.
On one GPU, even at full speed, it would take 584 years. How can you know that before you start?
It's a scenario Prof. Ding gives in her course, CSE 291P, as it turns to training: you, a huge job, and a deadline.
Why so huge? Bigger models and more data give lower loss. Those are the scaling laws, from 2020. So the jobs only grow.
Before you touch a single GPU, there is a quicker first step.
FLOPs are floating-point operations: the multiplies and adds a chip does. This model has 405 billion parameters, the numbers it learns, and it reads about 15 trillion tokens, pieces of words.
A 2022 rule of thumb, Chinchilla, says about 20 tokens per parameter. Llama 3 used about 37.
Now the rule. Training costs about six operations per parameter, per token. Where does six come from?
Going forward, every weight does a multiply and an add for every token. That's two.
Going backward costs twice that. Here is why, in her words.
One gradient for the input, one for the weights: how each number should change. Two plus four makes six.
So multiply. Six, times 405 billion, times 15 trillion. That's 3.645 times ten to the 25 operations.
The paper itself reports 3.8 times ten to the 25: the same rule, with its 15.6 trillion tokens. It's an estimate. It counts the big matrix multiplies and little else.
Picture that work as a mountain of ingredients, and one GPU as one cook at one stove.
One H100 GPU, using 8-bit numbers called FP8, peaks at 1,979 trillion operations a second. That's without sparsity, a trick for skipping zeros, and at 100 percent, all the time.
Divide. About 1.84 times ten to the ten seconds. About 584 years.
A GPU that started in the 1440s would just about be finishing.
But Llama 3 was trained on up to 16,000 H100s. Split the mountain that many ways, at full speed, and it's about 13 days.
Thirteen days. Easy? Then she asks the class.
Her slide hunts for the missing factor of four. First.
MFU, model FLOPs utilization, is the share of the peak you actually use. Llama 3 kept 38 to 43 percent. At 40 percent, it runs two and a half times slower.
Why not 100 percent? Cooks wait on each other, and on memory. Her list.

And things break. The paper gives no single total time. It reports a 54-day stretch of pre-training with 466 interruptions. 419 were unexpected, and about 78 percent of those were hardware, GPUs most of all.
Second. Llama 3 trained in 16-bit numbers, not FP8, and in 16-bit the H100 peaks at half its FP8 speed. Another two times.
Her slide rounds both factors to two: 13 days times four, about 54 days. With two and a half, it's nearer two months. Either way, weeks, not centuries.
The lesson. Count the FLOPs first, and the rest follows.
And the count says one GPU is hopeless. Training has to be spread over thousands of them. Next: what is inside a cluster like that.
